rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all eight compounds and identify the critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing late peaks. The retention pattern will guide subsequent gradient-window, slope, and temperature adjustments.

Only the earliest pair is unresolved, while the run already finishes comfortably within 10 minutes. Changing temperature alone tests whether selectivity can separate that pair without sacrificing the well-resolved remainder.
Lengthen the gradient one step to improve the earliest pair from R = 1.41 toward full resolution. Keep the favorable temperature, with ample time margin for the last peak to remain below 10 minutes.

The maximum CRF is achieved; now test a shorter fully resolved method. This gradient has a slope between injections 2 and 3, which should retain R above 1.5 for the critical pair while shortening the last-peak time.

Raise the gradient window by 0.05 while preserving injection 4's slope to test a faster fully resolved separation. This isolates the starting-composition effect on the critical early pair; injection 4 remains a fully resolved fallback.

Restore the lower starting fraction and use a slightly steeper slope than injection 4, targeting a faster separation with the critical pair still above R = 1.5. The final fraction remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition, keeping all peaks within the gradient.

Test a slightly steeper gradient, predicted to leave the critical early pair just above R = 1.5. The last peak may enter the final hold, so this run will establish whether the shorter gradient actually reduces its elution time.

With a maximum-score method secured, test the low-temperature selectivity regime for an alternative route to faster full resolution. This broad gradient should still elute all compounds safely and reveal whether cooling separates the critical pair in a different elution order.

Test whether modest warming separates the late cluster seen at 25 C while retaining the improved early-pair selectivity. A steeper gradient targets a shorter run and probes an alternative to the fully resolved 60 C method.

Test a shallower gradient to spread the late cluster at 30 C, while raising the starting fraction to offset the added retention time. This also probes whether the shifted solvent window improves early-pair selectivity in the low-temperature regime.

Raise temperature one step while holding injection 10's gradient fixed to separate the remaining late cluster and shorten retention. This tests whether 35 C provides a selectivity balance that resolves both the early pair and the late pairs.

Return to the best-performing temperature and test a slope of 0.085 organic fraction per minute, just steeper than injection 7. This probes the speed limit for full resolution of the early pair while avoiding a final-hold delay for the last peak.

Test whether a shallower slope restores full resolution at the higher starting fraction that failed in injection 5. This brackets the resolution boundary for a second gradient window while retaining the maximum-score methods already established.

Shift injection 11's gradient window upward while preserving its slope to test starting-composition selectivity at 35 C. The late pairs were resolved there; this run tests whether the early pair can improve while shortening the separation.

Reduce injection 11's slope from 0.10 to 0.075 per minute to improve its sole unresolved pair. This tests whether the 35 C selectivity regime can also achieve full resolution before 10 minutes, providing an alternative maximum-score method.

Slightly steepen injection 13's gradient from 0.0700 to 0.0708 per minute, testing whether its small resolution margin permits faster elution. Although the programmed gradient is longer, the last peak should elute slightly earlier and remain comfortably below 10 minutes.

Test a further upward shift in starting composition with a compensating shallower slope to resolve the early pair. This maps whether a narrower solvent window can offer a competitive fully resolved method; injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Trim injection 3's gradient to a shorter program with the same starting fraction and slope, placing the endpoint above the last peak's estimated elution composition. This should preserve its full-resolution margin and maximum CRF while reducing the programmed gradient duration and final organic fraction.

Lower injection 15's starting fraction while preserving its slope to improve the remaining early-pair resolution. The last peak is estimated to elute near 9.7 minutes, testing a lower-temperature maximum-score alternative without substantial truncation risk.

Test one temperature step below the fully resolved injection 18 to measure how much its critical-pair margin depends on operating at 60 C. Retention should remain below 10 minutes; the established maximum-score methods remain the fallback.

Refine the fully resolved 0.10-starting-fraction method with a shorter, narrower gradient and a slightly shallower slope than injection 13. This should preserve maximum CRF with a modest resolution margin and keep the last peak within the gradient.

Raise injection 7's endpoint one grid step to remove its final-hold delay and test the next faster six-minute gradient. The early pair may fall below R = 1.5; injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved fallback.

Back off to a shallower six-minute gradient, using the slope that gave R = 1.67 in injection 18. The lower endpoint will delay the last peak during the hold, but should retain maximum CRF if it elutes before 10 minutes.

Test a six-minute version of the fully resolved 0.10-starting-fraction window, with a slightly shallower slope than injection 21. The early pair should retain full resolution, while the last peak's hold-phase elution will determine whether this compact program preserves maximum CRF.

Use the final injection to test a slightly shallower version of injection 18, targeting more critical-pair resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. Maximum CRF is already secured, with injection 7 remaining the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
